specPoints.text: know that photographic film or a Geiger−Müller detector can detect ionising radiations
explain the sources of background (ionising) radiation from Earth and space

primer.text: Radiation is invisible, but not undetectable: photographic film darkens where radiation strikes, and the Geiger-Müller tube clicks for every count. Add the ever-present background from radon, cosmic rays and food, and every honest measurement starts by subtracting it.

lessons.title: Photographic film and the GM tube
lessons.opening: Two detectors cover the syllabus: photographic film, which darkens as it absorbs radiation and so monitors workers’ doses, and the Geiger-Müller tube, which turns each absorbed particle into an electrical pulse and a count rate. Closer to the source, higher the count.
keyPoints: Photographic film detects radiation by darkening when it absorbs it.
Film badges worn by radiographers record cumulative exposure between checks.
The Geiger-Müller tube transmits an electrical pulse for each radiation absorbed.
The count rate rises as the tube moves closer to the source.
The frequency of clicks tracks the intensity of the radiation arriving.

low.restatement: Film is a passive record — wear it, develop it, read the dose. The GM tube is active — it counts every hit with a click, and moving it closer raises the tally.
low.analogy: Film is a sunburn log of your day; the GM tube is a rain gauge ticking with every drop.
low.examPointer: Name the GM tube precisely (Geiger-Müller, GM tube, Geiger counter all accepted); never just "radiation detector".

medium.restatement: Film integrates dose through layered absorbers that discriminate radiation types, while the GM tube resolves counts in real time, so it serves rate measurements and corrected-count work. Distance matters because intensity falls with spreading, so geometry is part of every count comparison.
medium.analogy: Film is the month-end bank statement; the GM tube is the live payment alert on your phone — same information, different time resolution.
medium.examPointer: For "state a detector" questions give both film and GM tube; for rate questions the tube is the answer.

check.stem: How does photographic film indicate radiation exposure?

options.text: it darkens as it absorbs radiation
options.explanation: More absorbed radiation means a darker developed film.

options.text: it changes colour to blue only
options.explanation: Darkening, not a specific blue, is the signal.
Warming is not the detection mechanism.
Clicks belong to the GM tube.

check.stem: What does a Geiger-Müller tube do each time it absorbs radiation?

options.text: transmits an electrical pulse to a counting circuit
options.explanation: Each absorption generates one pulse — the count.
That is the film badge’s job.
The tube detects; it does not emit.
Nothing is stored; each event is counted.

check.stem: A GM tube is moved closer to a source. What happens to the count rate?

options.explanation: Closeness raises the intensity of radiation reaching the tube.
Falling is what happens when you move away.

options.text: it stays constant regardless of distance
options.explanation: Geometry matters — the syllabus says so.
Closeness maximises, not zeroes, the count.

check.stem: Why do radiographers wear film badges with layered absorbers?

options.text: the layers discriminate the dose delivered by different radiation types
options.explanation: Absorber layers let the developed film separate contributions.
Weight is not the design goal.

options.text: to make the film develop faster
options.explanation: Development speed is unrelated.
A badge monitors; it does not shield.

check.stem: Which detector gives an immediate count rate rather than a cumulative record?

options.explanation: The tube counts events as they arrive.
Film integrates until it is developed.
A box is shielding, not a detector.
Absorbers modify radiation; the tube measures it.

check.stem: Name two detectors of ionising radiation.
check.modelAnswer: Photographic film and the Geiger-Müller tube both detect ionising radiation.

check.stem: State what is meant by count rate.
check.modelAnswer: The count rate is the number of radiation detections per unit time recorded by a detector such as a GM tube.

check.stem: Explain why a film badge is checked regularly even though it gives no immediate reading.
check.modelAnswer: The badge accumulates darkening with every exposure, so regular checks read off the cumulative dose and flag over-exposure even though no single moment is timed.

check.stem: A GM tube records 480 counts in 2 minutes. Calculate the count rate in counts per second.

lessons.title: Background radiation and its sources
lessons.opening: Background radiation is the low-level bath of ionising radiation that surrounds us always. Natural contributors dominate: radon gas seeping from rocks, cosmic rays from space, carbon-14 in living material, and trace radioactivity in food and drink.
keyPoints: Background radiation is the low-level radiation present everywhere, all the time.
Radon gas, an alpha emitter, seeps from rocks and building materials.
Cosmic rays — fast protons from the sun and beyond — strike the atmosphere and produce gamma radiation.
All organic matter carries a trace of carbon-14.
Foods such as bananas carry tiny amounts of potassium-40.

low.restatement: Even with no source on the bench, the counter still ticks: radon from the ground, particles from space, a whisper of carbon-14 and potassium-40 in your lunch.
low.analogy: Background radiation is the faint hiss behind a radio station — always there, usually unnoticed, but real.
low.examPointer: Learn the big three natural sources (radon, cosmic rays, food and drink) — the exam hint names them as the significant contributors.

medium.restatement: Radon matters because it is inhaled — an alpha emitter inside the lungs delivers a large local dose. Cosmic protons spawn secondary gamma in the upper atmosphere, and biological carbon cycling keeps carbon-14 topped up in living tissue, so background dose is a geography-dependent mixture.
medium.analogy: The background is a stew with regional recipes: radon-heavy granite districts, mountain tops with extra cosmic seasoning.
medium.examPointer: Radon is the natural source with the health caveat (inhaled alpha) — pair those two facts if a question asks why radon matters.

check.stem: Which gas is a significant natural source of background radiation inside buildings?

options.explanation: Radon seeps from rocks and building materials.
Oxygen is not radioactive.
Helium is inert and not a background source.
Chlorine is not the named natural source.

check.stem: Cosmic rays reaching the atmosphere produce which radiation on collision with air molecules?

options.explanation: Fast protons colliding with air generate gamma.
Alphas come from nuclei, not from atmospheric collisions.
Sound is irrelevant to cosmic rays.
Gamma is the named product.

check.stem: Why does carbon-14 appear in all living things?

options.text: living organisms constantly replace their carbon, keeping the carbon-14 supply topped up
options.explanation: Biological carbon turnover maintains the trace level.

options.text: because carbon-14 is manufactured by cells
options.explanation: Cells do not make carbon-14.

options.text: because carbon-14 enters only through drinking water
options.explanation: The carbon cycle, not water alone, delivers it.
Nothing filters isotopes selectively like that.

check.stem: Which food-based isotope is named as a background contributor?

options.explanation: Bananas are the named example of food-borne radioactivity.
Carbon-12 is stable and not the named source.
Not the named natural food example.
Not the named food source.

check.stem: Why can inhaled radon be more hazardous than its low airborne concentration suggests?

options.text: because its alpha emissions act directly inside the lungs
options.explanation: An internal alpha emitter delivers a concentrated local dose.
Radon is colourless and odourless.
The hazard is inhalation, not food contamination.
Suffocation is not the named mechanism.

check.stem: Define background radiation.
check.modelAnswer: Background radiation is the ionising radiation present all around us at all times, from natural and artificial sources.

check.stem: List three natural sources of background radiation.
check.modelAnswer: Radon gas from rocks and buildings, cosmic rays from space, and radioactive material in food and drink (with carbon-14 in living matter).

check.stem: Explain why radon levels differ noticeably from one location to another.
check.modelAnswer: Radon comes from radioactive elements in rocks and soils, and geology varies regionally, so the gas seeping into buildings varies too.

check.stem: A patient is worried that all background radiation is man-made. Give a short, evidence-based correction.
check.modelAnswer: Most significant contributions are natural — radon from rocks, cosmic rays from space, and traces in food and drink — while man-made additions (medicine, fallout, accidents) exist but are not the whole picture.

lessons.title: Corrected count rate
lessons.opening: Honest counting subtracts the surroundings: measure the background with no source, then subtract it from every source reading to get the corrected count rate. Artificial sources — medicine, waste, fallout, accidents — add to the natural baseline but repeatable technique keeps them out of your data.
keyPoints: Measure the background count rate with no source present.
The corrected count rate is the source reading minus the background reading.
Repeating readings and averaging, or counting over longer intervals, improves accuracy.
Artificial background sources include nuclear medicine, nuclear waste, fallout and accidents.
A GM tube recording 24 counts per minute of background is 24/60 = 0.4 counts per second.

low.restatement: No source: 24 counts in a minute. With source: 285. Corrected: 285 − 24 = 261 per minute.
low.analogy: Weigh yourself holding the suitcase, then subtract your own weight — only the suitcase remains.
low.examPointer: Show the subtraction line explicitly — "corrected count rate" answers without the arithmetic can drop a mark.

medium.restatement: Because decay is random, a single-minute window is noisy; averaging repeats or extending the interval shrinks the uncertainty on both the background and the source measurements, so the corrected rate inherits the smaller error. Artificial contributions rarely vary over a session, which is what makes subtraction valid.
medium.analogy: Taring a kitchen scale: the bowl’s weight is constant during the bake, so subtracting it once is fair — provided nobody swaps the bowl mid-recipe.
medium.examPointer: If a question offers "repeat and average" as an accuracy improvement, take it — it is the stock answer here.

check.stem: The background count is 24 counts per minute. Express that per second.

options.explanation: That skips the division by 60.
Wrong factor of ten.
That would be 14.4 per minute.

check.stem: A source gives 285 counts per minute; background is 24. The corrected count rate is…

options.explanation: Addition is the wrong operation.
That ignores the background subtraction.
That is the background itself.

check.stem: Which is an artificial source of background radiation?

options.explanation: Medical uses of radiation add to background.
Radon is natural.
Cosmic rays are natural.
Carbon-14 is natural.

check.stem: Why does averaging repeated counts improve the accuracy of a corrected count rate?

options.text: because the randomness of decay makes single counts scatter
options.explanation: Averaging tames the random fluctuation.

options.text: because the source weakens while you count
options.explanation: That is a real effect but not the averaging rationale asked for here.

options.text: because the GM tube drifts between readings
options.explanation: Tube drift is not the named cause.
Background is steady over a session.

check.stem: Background is measured at 24 cpm. With the source at 1 m the reading stays at 24 cpm. What is the corrected count rate, and what does it mean?

options.text: 0 — the source’s radiation is fully absorbed by the air before the tube
options.explanation: The reading equals background, so the source contributes nothing at that distance.
The 24 is entirely background here.
Addition is meaningless here.
Corrected rates are not double-subtracted.

check.stem: Describe how to find the corrected count rate of a source.
check.modelAnswer: Measure the background count rate with no source present, measure the rate with the source present, and subtract the background from the source reading.

check.stem: Give the corrected count rate in counts per second for a source reading of 261 counts per minute.
Explain why the background measurement must be taken in the same place as the source measurements.
check.modelAnswer: Background varies with location, so a baseline measured elsewhere would not match the contributions present during the source readings, corrupting the subtraction.

check.stem: A GM tube records 160 counts in 5 minutes with no source, and 208 counts in 5 minutes with a source. Find both rates and the corrected count rate.
check.modelAnswer: Background: 160 ÷ 5 = 32 cpm; with source: 208 ÷ 5 ≈ 41.6 cpm; corrected: 41.6 − 32 = 9.6 cpm.

glossary.definition: The ionising radiation present at all times from natural and artificial sources.
The measured count rate with the background count rate subtracted.
High-speed particles from space that generate secondary radiation in the atmosphere.
A colourless, odourless radioactive gas, an alpha emitter, that seeps from rocks and building materials.

workedExample.prompt: A Geiger counter records 24 counts in one minute with no source present, and 285 counts in one minute with a source present. Find the background rate and the corrected count rate.
steps: Background: 24 counts per minute (24/60 = 0.4 counts per second).
Corrected count rate: 285 − 24 = 261 counts per minute.
In per-second form: 261/60 = 4.35 counts per second.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Background 24 cpm (0.4 cps); corrected count rate 261 cpm (4.35 cps).
